subject: anatomy
title: Muscles, nerves and vessels: general principles

steps.tx: Skeletal muscle fibres are arranged in different patterns. Fibres running parallel to the line of pull allow a long range of movement. **Pennate** muscles have fibres set obliquely to the tendon, which packs more fibres in and gives greater power but less range. Unipennate, bipennate and multipennate are the subtypes, depending on how many tendon sides the fibres attach to.
steps.say: Skeletal muscle fibres can run parallel to the line of pull or at an angle. Parallel fibres give a long range of movement. Pennate muscles have oblique fibres, which pack in more fibres and give greater power but a smaller range. The subtypes are unipennate, bipennate and multipennate, depending on how many sides of the tendon the fibres attach to.

steps.tx: Some muscles are classed by fibre shape. **Fusiform** muscles have a spindle shape, as in biceps brachii. **Triangular** or convergent muscles have fibres fanning into one tendon, as in temporalis. **Spiral** muscles have fibres twisted about 180 degrees between their attachments. Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, trapezius and supinator are spiral.
steps.say: Muscles are also classed by shape. Fusiform muscles are spindle shaped, such as biceps brachii. Triangular or convergent muscles fan into one tendon, such as temporalis. Spiral muscles have fibres twisted about one hundred and eighty degrees. Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, trapezius and supinator are classed as spiral in standard texts.

steps.tx: Some muscles have **dual or composite** supply, meaning two sets of fibres with one function but different nerves. Biceps femoris, adductor magnus, pectineus and flexor digitorum profundus are classic examples. Flexor digitorum superficialis and pronator teres are supplied by the median nerve alone. Pectoralis major is supplied by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves, not a dual supply.
steps.say: Some muscles have a composite or hybrid supply. Two sets of fibres do the same job but are supplied by different nerves. Biceps femoris, adductor magnus, pectineus and flexor digitorum profundus are classic examples. Flexor digitorum superficialis and pronator teres are supplied by the median nerve alone. Pectoralis major is supplied by its medial and lateral pectoral nerves.

steps.tx: A **dermatome** is the strip of skin supplied by a single spinal segment, which makes it useful for working out which root is affected. Landmarks worth memorising include the **umbilicus** at T10, the thumb at C6, the middle finger at C7 and the little finger at C8. The medial elbow relates to T1 while the medial arm relates to T2. Patchy numbness in these zones points towards a particular root rather than a peripheral trunk.
steps.say: A dermatome is the strip of skin supplied by one spinal segment, so numbness there can help you localise a lesion to a specific root. Handy landmarks include the umbilicus, which sits at T10. The thumb is C6, the middle finger is C7 and the little finger is C8. The medial elbow is T1 and the medial arm is T2. Sensory loss across these zones suggests a root problem rather than a peripheral nerve injury.

steps.tx: Blood vessels form **end arteries** where no meaningful anastomosis exists, so occlusion causes infarction; examples include the renal and splenic arteries. Actual anastomoses join arteries end to end, as in the palmar arch, circle of Willis and labial branches of the facial artery. **Potential anastomoses** join terminal arterioles and only dilate slowly, as in coronary and cortical cerebral branches.
steps.say: Some arteries are end arteries with no useful connection, so blockage causes tissue death. Actual anastomoses join arteries end to end, as in the palmar arch and circle of Willis. Potential anastomoses join terminal arterioles and open only slowly, as in the coronary and cerebral cortical arteries. Sudden occlusion can therefore overwhelm a potential anastomosis.
